subjects.name: Humanities

sections.title: Spaced Repetition and the Forgetting Curve
sections.description: Every memory starts fading the moment you stop using it.

sections.title: Active Recall: Why Testing Yourself Beats Rereading
sections.description: The most effective study technique ever measured feels harder and works worse in the moment — that is not a paradox, it is the finding.

sections.title: Interleaving: Why Mixed Practice Beats Blocked Practice
sections.description: Most people practice the way textbooks lay out chapters: one skill until it feels easy, then the next.

sections.title: Active Reading with SQ3R
sections.description: SQ3R — Survey, Question, Read, Recite, Review — is a reading strategy published by Francis P.

sections.title: Percentage, Ratio and Mental Math Shortcuts
sections.description: Percentages, ratios, and a toolkit of mental shortcuts power the arithmetic behind prices, tips, discounts, taxes, and news statistics.

sections.title: Deliberate Practice: The Anatomy of Getting Good
sections.description: Twenty years of driving does not make a race driver, and ten thousand casual rounds of golf does not make a champion.

sections.title: Angular Momentum and Rotational Dynamics
sections.description: Rotating bodies obey a mechanics built from angular analogues of force, mass, and momentum.

sections.title: Entropy and the Second Law
sections.description: The second law singles out which processes happen on their own: those that increase the total entropy of the universe.

sections.title: Special Relativity: Time, Length and the Speed Limit
sections.description: In 1905 a twenty-six-year-old patent clerk asked a disarmingly simple question: what does a beam of light look like if you race alongside it?

sections.title: Chemical Equilibrium and Le Chatelier’s Principle
sections.description: Most chemical reactions run both ways, and when forward and reverse rates equalize, concentrations settle into dynamic equilibrium.

sections.title: The Periodic Table’s Hidden Architecture
sections.description: The periodic table looks like wall decoration; it is closer to a map of the atom.

sections.title: How Stars Are Born, Live and Die
sections.description: Stars are not permanent ornaments; they are machines with fuel gauges, and a single number set at birth — mass — writes nearly the whole biography.

sections.title: CRISPR and the Mechanics of Gene Editing
sections.description: CRISPR-Cas9 turned genome editing from a specialist craft into a programmable routine.

sections.title: Action Potentials and Nerve Signaling
sections.description: Nerve impulses are electrical events built from moving ions.

sections.title: Photosynthesis: Light and Dark Reactions
sections.description: Photosynthesis converts light energy into chemical energy and feeds nearly every food web on Earth.

sections.title: Evolution by Natural Selection
sections.description: In 1858 Charles Darwin and Alfred Russel Wallace proposed a mechanism so compact it fits in one sentence: if individuals vary, if the variation is inherited, and if some variants leave more…

sections.title: The Immune System: Innate to Adaptive Defense
sections.description: Your body runs an open-border policy — food, air, cuts, kisses — and still keeps some thirty trillion of its own cells under protection.

sections.title: Ecosystems and the Flow of Energy
sections.description: A hectare of grassland intercepts a flood of sunlight, yet only a sliver ever becomes rabbit.

sections.title: The Derivative as a Limit
sections.description: The derivative answers one question with unreasonable power: at this exact instant, how fast is it changing?

sections.title: Bayes’ Theorem and Updating Beliefs
sections.description: Bayes’ theorem is the calculus of changing your mind: it says exactly how evidence should revise a prior belief into a posterior.

sections.title: Eigenvalues and What They Mean
sections.description: An eigenvector of a matrix is a direction its transformation leaves unchanged apart from stretching, and the eigenvalue is that stretch.

sections.title: Prime Numbers: The Atoms of Arithmetic
sections.description: Primes are the numbers that refuse to be broken apart: 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, and an endless procession afterward.

sections.title: Infinity and Different Sizes of Forever
sections.description: Galileo noticed that perfect squares are at once scarcer than whole numbers — thinning toward nothing as you climb — and exactly as numerous, since every whole number owns its own square.

sections.title: Graph Theory: From Königsberg to Networks
sections.description: In 1736 the citizens of Königsberg asked whether a Sunday stroll could cross each of the city’s seven bridges exactly once.

sections.title: Carbon Sinks and the Global Carbon Budget
sections.description: The global carbon budget is the balance sheet of the carbon cycle: human emissions from fossil fuels and land-use change, minus what ocean and land sinks reabsorb, leaves the rest to pile up in the…

sections.title: Planetary Boundaries and Safe Operating Space
sections.description: Planetary boundaries define a 'safe operating space' for humanity: nine Earth-system processes — climate change, biosphere integrity, land-system change, freshwater change, biogeochemical flows,…

sections.title: Soil Health and Regenerative Agriculture
sections.description: A healthy soil is not dirt but a living ecosystem — minerals, organic matter, roots, fungi, bacteria and animals — that cycles nutrients, stores water and resists erosion.

sections.title: The Water Cycle and Freshwater Scarcity
sections.description: The water cycle is Earth's endlessly repeating distillery: the sun evaporates about 500,000 cubic kilometres of water each year, mostly from the oceans, and rain and snow return nearly all of it.

sections.title: The Renewable Energy Transition
sections.description: The renewable energy transition is the attempt to move the world's energy system — still more than 80 percent fossil-fuelled — onto sunlight, wind, water, biomass and the Earth's internal heat.

sections.title: Biodiversity and the Sixth Extinction
sections.description: Life on Earth has endured five mass extinctions — the worst, at the end of the Permian 252 million years ago, erased roughly 90 percent of marine species.

sections.title: Hash Tables and Collision Resolution
sections.description: A hash table pushes each key through a hash function to choose an array slot, and that single idea buys average constant-time lookup, insertion and deletion — the reason it powers every language's…

sections.title: Backpropagation: How Neural Networks Learn
sections.description: Backpropagation is the bookkeeping trick that makes deep learning possible: it computes the gradient of a loss with respect to every weight using one forward pass and one backward sweep.

sections.title: Transformers and Attention: How Modern AI Reads
sections.description: Read a sentence and your eyes dart backwards and forwards — 'it' grabs its noun, a verb collects its subject, with no respect for order of encounter.

sections.title: Public-Key Cryptography and RSA
sections.description: Symmetric ciphers need a shared secret, which fails between strangers.

sections.title: Operating Systems: The Illusion of Many Machines
sections.description: A laptop juggling a browser, a video call and a music player seems to run them all at once — on a handful of cores, in memory none of them owns, touching devices none of them may address directly.

sections.title: Blockchains and Consensus Without a Boss
sections.description: Hand a stranger cash and the deal is done — the bill is in only one pair of hands.

sections.title: Feedback Control and PID Tuning
sections.description: A cruise control that ignores the road and a thermostat that only turns fully on or fully off both fail in instructive ways.

sections.title: Why Materials Fail: Stress, Fatigue and Fracture
sections.description: Materials fail in only a few fundamentally different ways, and engineers who can read those signatures prevent catastrophes.

sections.title: Three-Phase Power and Why the Grid Loves It
sections.description: Turn on a kettle and you see single-phase power at work; look at the transmission towers on the horizon and you are seeing three-phase.

sections.title: Why Bridges Stand: Loads, Stress and Safety Factors
sections.description: A bridge holds rush-hour traffic over a canyon for a century — through storms, heat waves and the slow creep of rust — and we walk onto it without a thought.

sections.title: Tolerances, Fits and the Reality of Measurement
sections.description: Ask a machine for a 20-millimetre shaft and it delivers 20.013, or 19.988, or 20.006 — never exactly 20, because nothing in manufacturing is exact: not the machine, not the tool, not the operator,…

sections.title: How Wings Really Lift: Aerodynamics Without Magic
sections.description: Ask a room why planes fly and someone will explain that air must travel farther over the curved top of the wing and therefore faster — the equal-transit-time story, which is wrong, and demonstrably…

sections.title: Lithium-Ion Batteries and the Chemistry of Charging
sections.description: A lithium-ion cell is a rocking chair for ions: lithium shuttles between a layered oxide cathode and a graphite anode, inserting itself into each host without destroying the crystal structure.

sections.title: How GPS Pinpoints You: Trilateration and Time
sections.description: Your phone locates itself to within a few meters by listening to whispers from satellites 20,000 kilometers overhead.
